# Drex Vertical Reframe

Turns long landscape video into vertical shorts automatically. The pipeline finds the moments worth watching, decides frame by frame which part of the picture to keep, and stitches those decisions into steady camera work. It currently works on two kinds of content: a football broadcast and a talking-head interview.

**Results page:** https://claude.ai/artifact/ReKDi7gGDdMBM9JRaekWxj. It has two tabs, `#football` and `#interview`, and is generated by `scripts/build_report.py`.

Built at the Nace AI Hackathon on **Drex Max v1.1** (`drex-max-v1.1`, the decision model) and **Nace NDI** (document intelligence: transcription and speaker diarization). `gemini-4-hydrogen` is the baseline.

## Why it matters

Creators publish long-form video in 16:9, but short-form reach lives in the 9:16 feeds of TikTok, Reels and Shorts. Reposting existing footage is the cheapest source of new content, but it doesn't work as is:

- **Only a third survives.** A full-height 9:16 frame keeps 32% of the width, and the other two-thirds gets cut.
- **The right third keeps moving.** In football you follow the ball on the attack, the goal on a shot, and the celebrating players after. In an interview you follow whoever is speaking.
- **Today it's manual.** Editors pick the moments and drag the crop frame by hand, shot by shot. That doesn't scale.

The results page puts three options side by side for both examples: reposting as is (the video fills about 32% of the screen), a center crop (loses the ball, or frames the gap between two people), and content-aware framing by Drex.

## Key ideas

- **Locating becomes multiple choice.** Drex has no bounding-box output. We draw numbered grid lines on the frame (vertical lines `0–16`, horizontal lines `A–J`) and ask `choice` questions such as "which line is the left edge of what must stay visible?" and "which line is the ball on?". The probability distribution over lines doubles as a confidence weight.
- **The expensive model only sees candidates.** Free signals (NDI transcript, crowd loudness, scene cuts) shortlist moments first. A 30-minute match needs about 70 Drex calls.
- **The camera language fits the content.**
  - Football uses a smooth follow-cam within a shot, a hard cut at shot boundaries, and a "ball must stay in frame" constraint.
  - Interviews use locked framing: one fixed position per shot, changed only by a hard cut.
- **Offline means anticipation.** A replay can see the future, so the camera starts moving before the shot instead of chasing the ball.

## Scenario 1: Football

**Test window:** Real Madrid 2–3 Barcelona (2017), video time 01:12:30–01:42:30. It contains four key moments: 73′ Rakitić goal, 77′ Ramos red card, 85′ James equalizer and 92′ Messi winner.

Pipeline (`reframe/pipeline.py`):

| Stage | What runs | Model calls |
|---|---|---|
| s0 structure | ffmpeg scene cuts, RMS loudness, commentary transcript (Nace NDI Parse; local Whisper `base.en` as fallback) | NDI |
| s1 events | Recall candidates from commentary keywords and crowd-noise peaks. Drex then gets 8 frames plus nearby commentary and answers `choice` (event type), `score` (excitement) and `choice` (peak frame) | Drex ×1 per candidate |
| s3 keyframes | One frame every 0.5 s inside each event clip, with the grid drawn on. Each frame gets 7 questions: shot type, the 4 edges of the keep region and the 2 focus lines (ball or face). 8 consecutive frames go in one request | Drex ×1 per 4 s of clip |
| s4 plan | Keep region → smallest 9:16 box (if the region is too wide, center on the focus point instead). Each shot is smoothed with a least-squares solve (time constant 0.8 s), weighted by normalized Drex confidence. Wherever the ball leaves the middle 80% of the crop, the solve is pinned and re-run (up to 3 rounds). Shot boundaries are hard cuts | – |
| render | `vertical_*.mp4` (720×1280 with audio) and `debug_*.mp4` (source with the Drex region and crop, next to the vertical output) | – |

Results on the 30-minute window:

- **Events:** 20 candidates → 8 clips, and all **4/4 key moments** are cut on time. Two of the 8 clips are a replay or celebration after a goal.
- **Cost and time:** 67 Drex calls and 983k input tokens, about **$0.03**. The whole window runs in under 3 minutes: s0 ~70 s (local transcription), s1 26 s, s3 73 s for 344 keyframes, and ~9 s render per clip.
- **Ball in frame:** the crop missed Drex's own ball reading **43% → 1%** of the time once the smoothing weights were fixed and the ball constraint added. They had been ~40,000× too weak, which flattened the camera path.
- **Grid feasibility (30 frames):** about 2.7k input tokens per frame and 1.7 s p50 latency. Subtracting Drex's uniform probability floor before decoding halved the positional uncertainty.

## Scenario 2: Talking-head interview

**Test video:** a 30-minute, three-person interview that was already edited (multi-camera). It produced 5 shorts of 19–37 s.

How it differs from football (`reframe/talk.py`):

| Step | Football | Interview |
|---|---|---|
| Find clips | Commentary keywords and crowd noise for recall; Drex checks 8 frames | NDI transcript with speaker diarization. Sentences go into Drex `state` as numbered lines. Drex scores 70 windows of 25–60 s as standalone shorts, then picks the opening and closing lines with `choice` |
| Where to look | Ball and nearby players on the grid | Drex says whether the speaker is left, center or right, then boxes their head and shoulders on the grid |
| Camera | Smooth follow, ball must stay in frame | Locked shot: one position per shot (confidence-weighted median), zero panning. It hard-cuts when the speaker changes or the face is out of frame for 2 s or more |

Results:

- **Cost:** about **$0.13** for 30 minutes: NDI $0.105 (10-minute chunks, because NDI's internal Whisper rejects files over 50 MB) plus Drex $0.023. End-to-end time is about 3.5 minutes.
- **Stability:** moving from the follow-cam to locked framing took in-shot panning from **1,492 → 0 px/min** and the time the crop is moving from **30% → 0%**. Face in frame went from 99% to 97%.

## Drex vs Gemini (`gemini-4-hydrogen`)

**Finding moments in the 30-minute match:**

| | On time | Calls | Latency | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Gemini native video (watches all 30 min, returns time ranges) | 1 / 4 | 1 | 23 s | $0.30 |
| Drex (NDI + crowd-noise recall, Drex confirms each) | **4 / 4** | 20 | 96 s | **$0.0013** |

Gemini described all three of its picks correctly, down to the scoreboard clock, but two of its video timestamps were off by about 9.2 minutes, so it cut the wrong footage.

**Framing on the same clips** (`scripts/gemini_aligned.py`): Gemini makes the per-frame decision from the s3 step on exactly the clips Drex cut, and the same planner and renderer are used for both. There are no human labels, so "in frame" is measured against both models' own readings, given below as Drex reference / Gemini reference.

| | Ball / face in frame | Decision time per clip | Cost per clip |
|---|---|---|---|
| Football · center crop | 49% / 60% | 0 | $0 |
| Football · Gemini | 68% / 100% | 56 s | $0.069 |
| Football · **Drex** | 99% / **73%** | **9 s** | **$0.0035** |
| Interview · Gemini | 97% / 96% | 48 s | $0.062 |
| Interview · **Drex** | 97% / 96% | **12 s** | **$0.0043** |

Drex Max v1.1 bills 30 nUSD per input token ($0.03 per million), and output is free. It uses about 36× more input tokens per clip than Gemini (it reads an image every 0.5 s), but the price per token is 50× lower. Drex per-clip cost and time are allocated by keyframe count from batched calls.

## Repository layout

| Path | What it is |
|---|---|
| `reframe/pipeline.py` | Football pipeline (s0–render) and the shared `stage0` and `render` |
| `reframe/talk.py` | Interview profile: transcript-based highlights, speaker-following, locked framing |
| `reframe/grid.py` | Grid overlay, edge/focus `choice` questions, probability decoding |
| `reframe/geometry.py`, `reframe/smooth.py` | Keep region → 9:16 box; weighted least-squares camera path |
| `reframe/nace.py` | Plain-HTTPS clients for Drex (`/v1/systemone`) and NDI (upload + Parse), with throttling and retry-after |
| `reframe/gemini.py`, `reframe/gemini_baseline.py` | Gemini native-video baseline |
| `scripts/gemini_aligned.py` | Gemini as crop director on the Drex clips (`--profile football\|talk`) |
| `scripts/compare.py`, `scripts/eval_path.py`, `scripts/eval_talk.py` | Label-free metrics: ball/face in frame, swings, pan, cost, latency |
| `scripts/grid_experiment.py`, `tools/label.html` | 30-keyframe grid study and the ground-truth labeling page |
| `scripts/build_report.py` (+ `report_template.html`, `overview_svg.py`, `scene_svg.py`) | Builds the results page from the runs |
| `demo/`, `scripts/serve_replay.py` | Portable Scene1 demo: offline replay (no key) and a live Streamlit app (see below) |
| `docs/` | API research, baseline design, Gemini baseline write-up, Modal research |

## Run it

```bash
# 1. Setup: ffmpeg + Python 3 with requests, numpy, pillow, openai-whisper
echo 'NACE_API_KEY=...'   >> .env    # Drex + NDI
echo 'GEMINI_API_KEY=...' >> .env    # baseline only

# 2. Football: 30-minute window of El Clásico 2017
python3 -m reframe.pipeline --video samples/football-keyframes/videos/el-clasico-2017.mp4 \
  --start 4350 --dur 1800 --name clasico

# 3. Interview: whole file
python3 -m reframe.talk --video interview-30min.mp4 --name interview

# 4. Gemini baseline on the same clips, then compare
python3 scripts/gemini_aligned.py --profile football --drex-run clasico   --name gemini_aligned_clasico
python3 scripts/gemini_aligned.py --profile talk     --drex-run interview --name gemini_aligned_interview
python3 scripts/compare.py

# 5. Results page → runs/report/index.html
python3 scripts/build_report.py --name clasico --variant g16f
```

- **Caching:** each stage caches its output under `runs/<name>/`. Delete a stage's JSON to rerun it. Every API call appends its usage and latency to `runs/usage.jsonl`.
- **Not committed:** `.env`, `runs/` and the source videos. The video sources are listed in `samples/football-keyframes/README.md`.
- **Rate limits:** requests are throttled to one every 0.6 s and honor `retry-after`. Shared venue Wi-Fi can trip the console's Vercel checkpoint (HTTP 403); wait briefly, or switch networks.

## Portable Scene1 demo

This branch includes everything needed to demonstrate the main pipeline: **six four-second input clips**, four real recorded runs, exact model-input JPEGs, responses, probabilities, crop previews and rendered videos. The full match, API keys and machine-specific paths are not included. Git LFS is not required.

```bash
git clone --branch demo/portable-scene1 --single-branch https://github.com/rederyang/drex-reframe.git
cd drex-reframe
```

### Offline replay — Python only, no key or network

```bash
python3 scripts/serve_replay.py
```

Open **http://127.0.0.1:8504/replay/**. Choose a clip and recorded focus, inspect the request/response and probabilities, or replay the source and vertical video together. This mode clearly displays `REPLAY` and sends no model requests. It needs only Python 3's standard library, with no pip packages or FFmpeg installation.

### Live demo — custom goals and real NACE calls

```bash
conda env create -f demo/environment.yml
conda activate drex-reframe-demo
cp .env.example .env
# Edit .env and set your own NACE_API_KEY.
streamlit run demo/app.py --server.address 127.0.0.1 --server.port 8503 --server.runOnSave false
```

Open **http://127.0.0.1:8503**. The Conda environment includes Python 3.12 and FFmpeg. If using an existing Python environment instead, install `demo/requirements.txt` and make `ffmpeg` / `ffprobe` available on PATH.

The English interface offers six fixed clips, preset goals and free text. Eight frames are sampled at 0.5-second intervals. One NACE request asks seven Choice questions per frame: shot type, four region edges and focus x/y. It directly calls `prepare_keyframe_batch()` / `detect_keyframe_batch()`, the existing probability decoder, `plan_clip()` and `render()` to produce a 720 × 1280 video with audio. The no-goal request matches the main implementation at `ab86fd8`; custom goals add context to state without replacing the workflow's logic. Switching frames or views never queries NACE. Changing the clip or goal invalidates the current result.

The live app reads **only this clone's** `.env` or `NACE_API_KEY` environment variable. Each new run is saved under ignored `runs/region_demo/<id>/`; no credentials are saved. All media defaults to `demo/assets/`. Processing times are local to each four-second clip; the UI retains its original Scene1 timestamp through the asset manifest.

### Bundled files and verification

| Path | Contents |
|---|---|
| `demo/assets/manifest.json` | Clip metadata, original offsets, cut points and SHA-256 checksums |
| `demo/assets/scene1/` | Six four-second MP4 clips, each under 2 MB |
| `demo/assets/recordings/` | Four real runs: model images, previews, vertical and comparison videos |
| `demo/replay/` | Standalone replay interface and sanitized recorded request/response JSON |
| `demo/environment.yml` | Live-demo environment including FFmpeg |

Run `python -m unittest discover -s tests -v` in the live environment to verify assets, decoding, rendering and UI behavior. The parity check against the original main stage is skipped only when its baseline commit is absent from a source export or shallow clone.

Maintainers can regenerate input clips with `python scripts/package_demo_assets.py --source-scene /path/to/original/scene1`. This command needs the original video **only for regeneration**, not for running either demo.
